To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the apparent polar wander (APW) curve for the interval ~800–1500 million years ago (Ma) for North America is a composite curve that includes the following: (1) a Sveconorwegian Loop, (2) an Atlantic Loop, (3) a Pacific Loop, (4) an El Paso Loop, (5) a Logan Loop, and (6) a Grenville Loop.

the North American apparent pole wander path for the interval 1.0–1.6 Gya is modified to include a Sveconorweigan Loop, and that the Hadrynian track is shortened by ~ 100 Ma, and is reversed to show that North America moved in a counterclockwise direction through the Hadrynian Loop.

the Grenville orogeny is not a single orogenic event, but is composed of several discrete orogenic events that occurred in two separate tectonic cycles; the Sveconorwegian orogeny is part of the second cycle; the El Paso and Aillik poles represent a new, previously unrecognized tectonic event; and the Hadrynian track is a minimum average continental motion track.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of apparent polar wander paths for the interval 0–2000 Ma.
the reconstruction of apparent polar wander (APW) curves for the interval 1.6–800 Ma for the Baltic Shield, Greenland, and North America.
the reconstruction of the apparent polar wander path of the Laurentia continent in the interval from ~800–1500 Ma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the North American apparent pole wander path for the interval 1.6–0.6 Ga is not well defined, and that there is no evidence for the existence of the Hadrynium Track, as defined by Irving (1977).
there was a major Grenvillian Loop, and a minor Logan Loop, and a major Hadrynian Track, with the latter being reversed in sense.

the North American apparent pole wander curve for the time interval ~ 1.6–1.0 Ga is a single, coherent, and continuous loop, the Hadrynian Loop, with the following properties: (1) the sense of motion is counterclockwise (i.e., the poles move in a counterclockwise sense about a fixed geographic pole), (2) the Hadrynian loop is a single, continuous loop, (3) the loop begins in the Pacific at
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
North America has been moving in an anticlockwise direction since the early Neoproterozoic.
the North American apparent paleomagnetic pole path for the interval 1.0–1.8 Ga is a combination of the Grenville and Logan Loop, and the Hadrynian, and El Paso, Stör, and Ailllk Bay tracks.
the apparent polar wander curve is a record of the motions of the North American plate with respect to a fixed geographic pole.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the apparent polar wander curve is a useful tool for understanding the geodynamic evolution of continents.
the paleomagnetic record of North America is not in conflict with a supercontinent scenario for the interval 1.6–1.0 Ga, as has been suggested.

the apparent polar wander curve of North America for the interval 1500–800 Ma can be interpreted as the result of a combination of plate tectonic motions and the rotation of Laurentia about a pole in the North Atlantic.
